articles.title: We gave our MCP server an undo button
articles.summary: Letting an AI agent change your product's settings is only reasonable if you can take it all back. So every change our MCP server makes goes into a run that can be undone in one step. This is how it works, and the decisions that turned out to be hard. In July 2025, Replit's AI agent deleted a company's production database during a code freeze, then told the user the data couldn't be recovered. It could. Replit had a rollback, and the user restored everything from a checkpoint. The agent just didn't know the feature existed. Two lessons from that story shaped what we built: the agent has to know that undo exists, and people have to be able to undo without asking the agent. We build Privatrak, a cookieless analytics tool. Its MCP server lets Claude, Cursor or Codex do more than read your analytics. Developers and autonomous engineering teams run multi-agent swarms in parallel: one agent refactors legacy code, a second generates unit tests, a third updates architectural documentation, and a fourth audits security vulnerabilities. What AIPass is AIPass is a framework for Claude Code. It turns single Claude Code sessions into a team of agents that persist. Each agent is a directory on your disk holding, among other things, an identity file, memory files it reads every time it wakes, a mailbox, and standing instructions that hooks inject into every session. When a session ends, the agent does not. The next session starts by reading what the last one wrote. All the agents work on the same filesystem as you, with no per-agent sandbox or worktree. articles.summary: Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM-based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM-guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset types. We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. First, we propose Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which leverages existing procedural algorithms to create novel, photorealistic assets while preserving editability and seed-based diversity. articles.title: Manga2Animate: An Agentic Framework for Faithful Manga Animation with Script and Storyboard Planning
articles.summary: Adapting existing manga into coherent animation that stays faithful to the source is a valuable yet challenging task. Existing methods either access the manga mainly through text, losing its characters and art style, or feed manga pages directly into video generation models, which misinterpret the manga's structure and produce incorrect storylines. In this paper, we propose Manga2Animate, a multi-agent framework that grounds every stage of generation in the source manga. We decompose the task into two intermediate representations, an animation script and a visual storyboard. Each representation is produced by a creator agent and reviewed against the source panels by a paired reviewer agent. We tailor representation-specific selection and dual-level feedback to progressively refine both before synthesizing the final animation. articles.title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
articles.summary: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. articles.title: OpenCode Told 1.4% of Console Users to Revoke Their OpenAI and Anthropic Keys
articles.summary: Book: LLM Observability Pocket Guide Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub The subject line was "Action Required: Potential provider key breach." On October 17, some OpenCode Console users opened an email that said: "We identified unauthorized access to a legacy system that we were in the process of decommissioning." Security researcher Matt Johansen posted a screenshot of it to X at 15:30 UTC with the line "Confirmed. OpenCode hacked. Keys stolen." The next sentence in that email is the one that matters if you use OpenCode Console: "Third party provider keys (eg OpenAI, Anthropic) saved in your workspace may have been exposed." At 18:08 UTC, OpenCode confirmed it on X: "We had a security breach last night related to a large scale distillation attack." The company put the impact at 1.
